analysis.one_liner: Gives workers job-protected leave for a new child, a family member's serious illness, or their own serious health condition.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared a Senate committee with bipartisan support and sat on the Senate calendar for a floor vote that never happened before the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require employers with 20 or more employees at a worksite to give eligible workers up to 10 weeks of unpaid family leave for a birth, adoption, foster placement, or to care for a child or parent with a serious health condition, and up to 13 weeks of unpaid medical leave for the worker's own serious health condition. Workers would get their job back, or an equivalent one, when they return, and their health insurance would continue during the leave. It would also extend the same rights to federal employees. The leave is unpaid unless the worker substitutes accrued paid vacation or sick leave.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who have been on the job at least 12 months at an employer with 20 or more employees at a worksite, when they have a baby or adopt a child, need to care for a sick child or parent, or face their own serious illness. Federal civil service employees get the same rights.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers needing leave for family or illness

how_it_helps.text: Entitles eligible employees to 10 workweeks of family leave during any 24-month period for a birth, adoption or foster placement, or to care for a child or parent with a serious health condition.
Entitles an employee who cannot work because of a serious health condition to up to 13 workweeks of temporary medical leave in a 12-month period.
Guarantees that an employee returning from leave is restored to their original position or an equivalent one with the same pay, benefits, and conditions, and that accrued benefits are not lost.
Requires the employer to maintain the employee's group health insurance coverage during the leave on the same terms as if the employee had kept working.

Makes it unlawful for an employer to interfere with these rights or retaliate against workers who file charges or testify, with enforcement by the Secretary of Labor and by private civil lawsuits carrying wages lost, liquidated damages, and attorneys' fees.
Extends the same family and medical leave rights to federal civil service employees, with job protection and the option to continue federal health benefits enrollment.
The bill's stated findings are that many workers must choose between job security and caring for family, and that caregiving burdens fall disproportionately on women.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 20 or more employees at a worksite would bear the cost of holding positions open for weeks at a time, continuing health insurance for workers on leave, training temporary replacements, and processing certifications and second opinions. The government would bear the cost of a new study commission and Labor Department enforcement.

drawbacks.text: The leave is unpaid. Workers may substitute accrued vacation, personal, or sick leave, but an employer is not required to pay for the leave, so many low-wage workers cannot afford to use the job protection the bill provides.

The bill covers only employers with 20 or more employees at one worksite and only employees with 12 months of service and at least 900 hours in the past year, leaving out workers at small firms and newer employees.
When a husband and wife work for the same employer, the two of them together may be limited to a combined 10 workweeks of family leave in 24 months.

Employers would face real costs: holding jobs open, continuing health coverage, and covering work during absences. The bill tries to limit abuse through medical certification, employer-paid second and third opinions, and recertification, but the compliance burden falls on business.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is genuine: workers get to keep a job through a birth or a family medical crisis, and employers absorb the cost of covering the absence. The bill tries to soften the burden by keeping the leave unpaid, allowing paid-leave substitution, excluding small employers, and requiring medical certification. Its biggest weakness is that an unpaid mandate helps least the workers who most need it, since a family living paycheck to paycheck may be unable to take weeks without pay.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee approved the bill and put it on the Senate's calendar of business in July 1989, but no one ever brought it to the floor for a vote before the Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Introduced February 2, 1989 by Senator Dodd of Connecticut with 20 original cosponsors including three Republicans, and read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources.
The committee ordered the bill reported favorably without amendment on April 19, 1989, and reported it to the Senate on July 13, 1989 with written report No. 101-77.
On July 13, 1989 the bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders, meaning it was waiting for floor time and a vote.
No further action was taken; the bill died on the calendar when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have faced the new leave, job-restoration, and health-coverage obligations are better off because the bill never came to a vote. Workers needing job-protected family and medical leave gained nothing in this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who avoided the leave mandate

for.name: Sen. Christopher Dodd
for.role: U.S. Senator from Connecticut, lead sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Family and Medical Leave Act of 1989 on February 2, 1989.

for.name: Sen. Edward Kennedy
for.role: Chairman, Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill to the Senate without amendment on July 13, 1989 after the committee ordered it reported favorably.

for.name: 3 of 45 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: Senate floor leadership
against.role: Controlled which calendar bills received floor time in the 101st Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote after it sat on the legislative calendar from July 1989 until the Congress ended.

against.name: President George H.W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Opposed a mandated family and medical leave law; his administration pressed against the mandate, and he later vetoed successor versions in the next Congress.

against.name: Business and employer groups
against.role: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and allied employer associations
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against mandated family leave on cost grounds during the multi-year fight over the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan at sponsorship: 21 of 55 Senate Democrats and 3 of 45 Senate Republicans cosponsored, and the committee reported the bill favorably, but the bill never reached a recorded vote, so the floor split was never tested.

industries.industry: U.S. employers (firms with 20 or more employees at a worksite)
industries.note: The bill would require them to hold jobs open for weeks of family or medical leave, continue health coverage during the leave, and manage certifications and temporary coverage, all at their own expense. Because the leave is unpaid, their direct wage cost is limited, but replacement and benefits costs are real.

Employers must keep group health coverage in force for workers on leave, so premiums and coverage continue rather than lapsing, and federal employees could continue their plan enrollment while on leave.

Employers covering weeks-long absences would rely more on temporary and contingent workers, though the bill also lets leave be taken intermittently or on a reduced schedule, which spreads the disruption.
